courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: Magnetic flux Phi = B.A = B*A*cos(theta), measured in webers (1 Wb = 1 T*m^2 = 1 V*s), in which theta is the angle between B and the NORMAL to the surface, so that the flux is a maximum B*A when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to B and exactly zero when the plane of the coil contains B, and the flux linkage of a coil of N turns is N*Phi.

Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, emf = -N d(Phi)/dt in volts, which makes the induced emf depend on the RATE OF CHANGE of the flux and not on the field, the flux or the motion, so that the flux through a circuit can be changed in exactly three ways - by changing B, by changing the enclosed area A, or by changing the orientation theta - and a stationary coil in a rising field has an emf while a coil drifting inside a uniform field has none.

Lenz's law, which is what the minus sign records: the induced current flows in the sense whose own magnetic field opposes the CHANGE in flux that produced it, so an approaching north pole meets an induced north pole and a receding north pole meets an induced south pole; it follows from conservation of energy, and the associated sign convention ties the positive normal, the sign of the flux and the positive sense of circulation together by the right hand.

Motional emf, emf = B*L*v for a rod of length L moving at speed v perpendicular to B, with the induced current I = B*L*v/R producing a retarding force F = B*I*L = B^2*L^2*v/R that always opposes the motion, so that the mechanical power supplied F*v equals the electrical power dissipated I^2*R exactly.

The a.c. generator, in which a coil of N turns and area A rotating at angular speed omega gives Phi = B*A*cos(omega*t) and emf = N*B*A*omega*sin(omega*t) with peak value N*B*A*omega, omega = 2*pi*f and rms value peak/sqrt(2), the emf being zero when the flux is greatest (plane perpendicular to B) and greatest when the flux is zero (plane containing B).

Self-inductance L = N*Phi/I in henries, with back-emf = -L dI/dt, stored energy 0.5*L*I^2 and L = mu_0*mu_r*N^2*A/l for a solenoid; and mutual inductance M = N2*Phi21/I1 with emf2 = -M dI1/dt, the reciprocity theorem M12 = M21, the coupling coefficient in M = k*sqrt(L1*L2), and the ideal transformer relations Vs/Vp = Ns/Np and Vp*Ip = Vs*Is, which work on a.c. only because a steady current gives d(Phi)/dt = 0.

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: The definite integral (integral from a to b of f(x) dx) is defined as the limit of Riemann sums (sum over i = 1 to n of f(x_i*) * delta_x) with delta_x = (b - a)/n, and it measures SIGNED area: strips lying below the x-axis contribute negatively, so a value of zero means the parts above and below cancel rather than that no region exists.

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in its evaluation form states that if f is continuous on [a, b] and F is ANY antiderivative of f there, then (integral from a to b of f(x) dx) = F(b) - F(a); the arbitrary constant cancels in the subtraction, so a definite integral is a number and never carries a + C.

The area actually bounded by a curve y = f(x) and its axis of definition on [a, b] is (integral from a to b of |f(x)| dx): find the roots of f inside the interval, split there, integrate each piece and add the magnitudes, because |integral of f| under-reports whenever f changes sign.

The area between two curves is (integral from a to b of [top - bottom] dx), where the strip height is a difference of y-values and is therefore valid whatever the signs of the two functions - a region lying entirely below the x-axis needs no translation upward.

When two curves intersect, the solutions of f(x) = g(x) supply the limits of an enclosed region, and any intersection strictly inside the interval forces a split at which the order of subtraction reverses; a single integral with a modulus taken at the end is wrong, most starkly for y = x^3 and y = x on [-1, 1] where it gives 0 for an area of 1/2.

When the left and right boundaries of a region are single functions of y while its top or bottom boundary changes formula partway, horizontal strips give A = (integral from c to d of [x_right(y) - x_left(y)] dy) as one integral where vertical strips would need two; the same setup gives the area between a curve and the y-axis, which is (integral of x dy) and not (integral of y dx).

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: An array is a type of data structure that can store a fixed-size sequential collection of elements of the same type; it is declared in C as datatype arrayName[arraySize], so that int a[10]; defines an array of size 10, that is, a block of 10 consecutive int-sized locations whose count is settled at the declaration and never changes while the programme runs.

An array may be initialised one element at a time or in a single statement such as double salaries[5] = {1000.0, 2.0, 3.4, 7.0, 50.0};, subject to the one-sided rule that the number of values between the braces cannot be larger than the number of elements declared between the square brackets - too few is legal and the remaining elements become 0 - and if the size is omitted, as in double salaries[] = {1000.0, 2.0, 3.4, 7.0, 50.0};, an array just big enough to hold the initialisation is created.

An element is accessed by indexing the array name, and because the elements are sequential and all of the same width the index is an offset computed as start-of-array plus index times element width rather than a position counted from one; the first legal index is therefore 0 and the largest is one less than the declared count, so salaries[2] is 3.4 and salaries[5] lies one element past the end of the block, where C stores no length, performs no bounds check, and neither diagnoses nor prevents the access.

A multi-dimensional array is defined using multiple adjacent square brackets and may be initialised with values enclosed in curly braces, and to access an element the correct notation encloses each subscript in a separate pair of square brackets, as m[1][2] and never m[1,2]; each subscript carries its own independent bound, and only the leftmost dimension may be omitted from a declaration because the compiler can count the rows but must know the row width in order to compute an address.

Recursion is a process in which a function indirectly and directly calls itself within its own function block, allowing a problem to be broken into one or more sub-problems similar in form to the original; a recursive function has a base case that handles the smallest input and returns without recursing and a recursive case that produces a smaller version of the original problem together with the work of combining, and it terminates only if every recursive call also makes progress that actually lands on the base case.

Recursion is classified on two independent axes - direct, which contains an explicit call to itself, against indirect, where a function calls another function which eventually calls it back; and tail, which has no pending operations to be performed on return from a recursive call, against non-tail, which has - and the deck's factorial comparison shows the trade: the iterative version has two local variables, three statements and saves its solution in an intermediate variable before returning it, while the recursive one has none, has one, and returns its result as a single expression, because recursion simplifies the function by making the computer do more work (one live stack frame per outstanding call) while we do less.

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Experiment to determine the magnetic dipole moment M and the pole strength m of a bar magnet using a tangent galvanometer, a metre stick and the bar magnet itself, with the galvanometer used purely as a mounted compass since no current flows in its coil.

The tangent law, which states that a freely pivoted magnetic needle acted on by two mutually perpendicular horizontal fields settles along their resultant so that B = B_H tan(theta), where B_H (written H_0 in the deck) is the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field, taken as 40 x 10^-6 T, and theta is the deflection from the undeflected north-south position; the same law gives tan(theta) proportional to I when the instrument is used as an ammeter.

The end-on (Tan A) axial field of a bar magnet of pole strength m and half-length L at a distance d from its centre, B = (mu_0/4pi) x 2Md/(d^2 - L^2)^2 with M = 2mL, derived either by adding the inverse-square fields of the two poles or by the deck's Biot-Savart integration along the magnet, and its far-field limit B = (mu_0/4pi) x 2M/d^3 which this experiment deliberately does not use.

The measurement routine: the magnet is placed on the metre stick east-west at d = 50 cm from the centre of the tangent galvanometer and the deflection angles theta_1 and theta_2 (both ends of the needle) are recorded, then theta_3 and theta_4 after clicking REVERSE POLARITY, and the whole set is repeated at d = 45, 40, 35 and 30 cm and then again with the magnet on the opposite side to give theta_5 to theta_8, so that eight angles per distance cancel needle eccentricity, scale zero error and off-centre placement.

The analysis: averaging the eight angles to theta_AV, plotting tan(theta_AV) against d/(d^2 - L^2)^2 to obtain a straight line through the origin of gradient s = mu_0 M/(2 pi B_H), and hence M = 2 pi B_H s/mu_0 = s x B_H x 5 x 10^6 in A m^2 followed by the pole strength m = M/(2L) in A m; with the deck's own data (theta_AV = 12.00 deg at d = 50 cm to 44.00 deg at d = 30 cm, magnet 10 cm long) this gives s = 0.0243 m^3, M = 4.9 A m^2 and m = 49 A m.

courses.name: Nigerian Peoples and Culture
weekTopics: Popular culture defined as the traditions and material culture of a particular society and as media with mass accessibility and appeal, a term coined in the mid-19th century for the cultural traditions of the people in contrast to the official culture of the state or governing classes.

The rise of popular culture, traced by scholars to the middle class generated by the Industrial Revolution, the working classes who moved into urban environments, and the post-World War II innovations in mass media, coinciding with the rise of capitalism until its meaning merged with mass culture, consumer culture, image culture and media culture.

The four epochal stages of popular Nigerian music: the traditional First Wave of 1950-67 (Juju, Apala, Highlife; I.K. Dairo, Haruna Ishola, Bobby Benson), the Second Wave of 1967-80 (Highlife's revival, Fela's Afrobeat, upper-class Juju under Obey and King Sunny Ade, and Fuji as a fusion of Apala and Ajisari under Barrister and Kollington), the Third Wave of 1980-90 (Waka, Yo Pop, Afro Juju, the Island and Virgin signings, the Ajegunle sound, and the dwindling identity crisis) and the Fourth Wave of 1992 to the present (Remedies, Plantashun Boiz, Styl Plus, Psquare, Mo'Hits Crew).

Police brutality in Nigeria as a long-standing pattern of excessive force, extrajudicial killings, harassment and abuse of power, explained by Moses Ochonu as a police force never decolonised from colonial suppression of revolts and by Abimbola Oyarinu as SARS being born of post-oil-boom economic turmoil, the depreciating naira, the civil war, the Structural Adjustment Programme and poor leadership.

The #EndSARS crisis as a decentralised social movement that began as a Twitter hashtag in 2017 and metamorphosed into a three-week crisis in October 2020, triggered immediately by a video of a police officer shooting an unarmed civilian, broadening into demands for good governance and transparency, and ending with the Nigerian Army firing on protesters at the Lekki toll gate on 20 October 2020.

The impact of #EndSARS on the 2023 general elections and youth political awakening: a record 10 million new registered voters, around 76 percent of them young people and 40 percent of those students, 87.2 million of 93.4 million registered voters collecting Permanent Voter Cards, yet a countrywide turnout of only 29 percent, the lowest in six decades of independence.

courses.name: Communication in English II
weekTopics: Inductive reasoning is defined as a form of reasoning in which the conclusion is considered likely or probable but not certain given the premises, working by recognising patterns in specific observations or past experiences and generalising from them, as in the three-stage swan example that moves from 'My swan is white' to 'Every observed swan is white' to 'Therefore, all swans are white'.

Deductive reasoning is defined as a form of reasoning in which the conclusion is necessarily true if the premises are true, and is illustrated by the categorical syllogism (all mammals have a backbone; whales are mammals; therefore whales have a backbone), by modus ponens (affirming the antecedent of a true conditional forces the consequent), by modus tollens (if A then B; not B; therefore not A), and by mathematical proof from axioms and established rules.

The lesson treats three types of inductive reasoning in detail - generalisation (a broad statement about a group based on specific observations, such as 'Many people wear sunglasses and hats on sunny days'), analogical reasoning (concluding about one thing from its similarities to another, such as a new breed of cat likely being a good hunter), and statistical reasoning (a 70 percent probability that Candidate A wins, drawn from past results and current polling) - and sets causal inference, prediction, abductive reasoning and enumerative induction for further reading.

The strength of an inductive conclusion depends on the quantity and quality of the evidence, so induction predicts rather than guarantees (historical weather data make winter cold likely but say nothing certain about a specific day; a recent rise in mosquito activity makes a disease outbreak likely), and its named weaknesses are sampling bias, reliance on incomplete data, coincidental patterns, and evidence whose quality and quantity can vary.

A deductive argument is valid when its conclusion follows logically from its premises and sound when it is valid and its premises are true, so certainty is guaranteed only by a sound argument; validity is an all-or-nothing property of form that never applies to inductive arguments, which are instead judged strong or weak, deduction being 'all or nothing' logic while induction acknowledges nuance and probability.

courses.name: Introduction to Web Technologies
weekTopics: Server-side (backend) programming languages are languages designed specifically for server-side scripting, running on a web server to process requests from client-side applications and handling database operations, user authentication and the generation of dynamic content for the client to render; they matter for dynamic content generation, data processing, user authentication, security against vulnerabilities such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, and scalability under many concurrent users.

The five named server-side languages each carry one distinguishing characteristic that decides when it is chosen: Python is versatile and used with Django and Flask, Ruby is renowned for elegant syntax and used with Ruby on Rails, PHP is known for simplicity and is often embedded directly in HTML, Node.js brings JavaScript to the server and is highly efficient for real-time applications thanks to its event-driven non-blocking I/O model handling many concurrent connections, and Java is renowned for reliability and scalability and is used with Spring.

A server environment (server infrastructure or server stack) is the collection of hardware, software and networking components enabling a server to function, comprising server hardware, storage, networking equipment, an operating system, server software, networking configuration, security measures and monitoring and management tools, and it is illustrated by four worked stacks: a LAMP web server environment (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP with phpMyAdmin and Fail2ban), a microservices application environment using Docker for containerisation and Kubernetes for orchestration with Prometheus, Grafana and Helm, a PostgreSQL database server environment with encryption at rest, pgAdmin and pgBadger, and an AWS cloud environment using EC2, RDS, Lambda, VPC, IAM, WAF, CloudWatch and Elastic Beanstalk.

Database management is the efficient and secure storing, organising, retrieving and managing of data, resting on the key terms database, DBMS, data model, SQL, schema, normalization, indexing and ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability), and practised through data modelling, normalization, indexing, security, performance optimisation, replication and high availability, and horizontal scaling by adding servers or vertical scaling by upgrading them, and it is embodied in five common systems: MySQL, PostgreSQL and Oracle Database as ACID-compliant relational systems for small-to-medium web databases, large-scale complex data models, and enterprise applications and data warehouses respectively, MongoDB as a schema-less document-oriented NoSQL system for unstructured or semi-structured data, and Redis as an in-memory NoSQL key-value store for caching, real-time analytics and message brokering.

An Application Programming Interface is a set of rules, protocols and tools letting different software applications communicate, defined by endpoints (specific URLs or URIs), the HTTP methods GET to retrieve, POST to create, PUT to update and DELETE to remove data, requests and responses carrying status information, data and headers in JSON or XML, plus authentication, rate limiting and documentation; APIs deliver interoperability, modularity, scalability, ecosystem expansion and a clean separation of front end from back end.

API development proceeds through defining the purpose, designing endpoints and data formats, implementing routes and handlers, testing success and error cases, documenting, securing with authentication and authorisation, and versioning for backward compatibility, while API integration covers social media, payment gateway, mapping, cloud storage and third-party data scenarios under best practices of reading documentation, handling errors, respecting rate limits, validating data, authenticating properly, testing thoroughly and tracking version updates, with cookies and session management maintaining user state across otherwise independent HTTP requests between a frontend of HTML, CSS and JavaScript and a backend of PHP, Rails, Django, Node.js, ASP.NET Core and a database.

Finding limits by setting f(x) = 0 and testing an interior point. Splitting at a root when the curve crosses the axis inside the interval.

The two-curve rule A = ∫ₐᵇ(f(x) − g(x))dx, with its condition f(x) ≥ g(x) and limits from f(x) = g(x).

questions.q: The area between y = 9 − x² and the x-axis is to be found, and no interval is given. Solve 9 − x² = 0 to find the limits of integration.
questions.concept: Limits of integration from f(x) = 0
questions.why:
The curve cuts the axis where 9 − x² = 0, so x² = 9 and x = −3 or x = 3. The region is enclosed between these two roots, so the limits are −3 and 3.

x = 3 only forgets the negative square root; x = 0 and x = 9 treats the expression as x(9 − x); x = −9 and x = 9 forgets to take the square root of 9.

questions.q: The curve y = x² + 1 lies above the x-axis. Find the area between the curve and the x-axis from x = 1 to x = 2.
questions.concept: Area under a curve above the x-axis
questions.why:
f ≥ 0, so A = ∫₁²(x² + 1)dx = [x³/3 + x]₁² = (8/3 + 2) − (1/3 + 1) = 14/3 − 4/3 = 10/3 square units.

14/3 forgets to subtract the value at the lower limit; 7/3 integrates x² alone and drops the + 1; 3 substitutes the limits into x² + 1 itself instead of into its antiderivative.

questions.q: f(x) = x² − 4 on [0, 1]. Evaluate f at the test point x = 1/2, and hence write the area between the curve and the x-axis on [0, 1] as an integral.
questions.concept: Choosing the area formula by a sign test
questions.why:
f(1/2) = (1/2)² − 4 = 1/4 − 4 = −15/4 < 0, and f has no root inside [0, 1] (its roots are ±2), so f ≤ 0 on the whole interval. Below the axis the integral is negative, so the area is its modulus: A = |∫₀¹(x² − 4)dx| = |1/3 − 4| = 11/3.

The second option keeps the negative integral as the area; the third gets the sign of f(1/2) wrong and so picks the wrong case; the fourth evaluates 2x − 4 instead of x² − 4 at the test point.

questions.q: The line y = x + 2 and the parabola y = x² enclose a region. Find the x-values where the two curves meet.
questions.concept: Intersection points of two curves
questions.why:
Set the curves equal: x + 2 = x², so x² − x − 2 = 0, (x − 2)(x + 1) = 0, giving x = −1 and x = 2. These are the limits of integration for the enclosed region.

x = 1 and x = −2 has the factor signs backwards; x = 2 only drops the negative root; x = ±√2 loses the x term and solves x² = 2.

questions.q: y = 6 − x and y = x² meet at x = −3 and x = 2. Using the test point x = 1, write the integrand for the area between the curves on [−3, 2].
questions.concept: Choosing top minus bottom by a test point
questions.why:
At x = 1: 6 − 1 = 5 and 1² = 1, so the line is on top. The strip height is top minus bottom, (6 − x) − x² = 6 − x − x², which is what is integrated from −3 to 2.

(6 − x) + x² adds the curves instead of subtracting; x² − (6 − x) subtracts in the wrong order and gives a negative result; 6 − x forgets to subtract the lower curve at all.

questions.q: On [0, 2] a curve y = f(x) runs below the x-axis, crosses it once at x = 1, then rises above it. ∫₀¹f(x)dx = −2/3 and ∫₁²f(x)dx = 4/3. Find the total area between the curve and the axis on [0, 2].
questions.concept: Adding areas across an axis crossing
questions.why:
Split at the crossing and take the modulus of the piece below the axis: A = |−2/3| + 4/3 = 2/3 + 4/3 = 2 square units.

4/3 counts only the piece above the axis; −2/3 is the piece below with no modulus; 2/3 is the single integral ∫₀²f(x)dx = −2/3 + 4/3, in which the two pieces partly cancel.

questions.q: The graph of y = g(x) on [0, 4] is a straight line from the point (0, 4) down to the point (4, 0). Find the area between this line and the x-axis.
questions.concept: Setting up an area from a described graph
questions.why:
The line has intercept 4 and gradient (0 − 4)/(4 − 0) = −1, so g(x) = 4 − x, which is ≥ 0 on [0, 4]. A = ∫₀⁴(4 − x)dx = [4x − x²/2]₀⁴ = 16 − 8 = 8 square units, which agrees with the triangle formula ½ × 4 × 4.

16 integrates the constant 4 alone and forgets the −x; 4 halves the triangle a second time; −8 integrates x − 4, the line written upside down.

questions.q: f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b], and the whole region between the two curves lies below the x-axis. Which expression gives the area between the curves?
questions.concept: Area between curves below the x-axis
questions.why:
The height of a vertical strip is the difference of the two y-values, f(x) − g(x), which is ≥ 0 wherever f is on top, whether or not the y-values themselves are negative. So A = ∫ₐᵇ(f(x) − g(x))dx with no modulus and no sign change. For example f(x) = −x² and g(x) = −4 on [−2, 2] give ∫(4 − x²)dx = 32/3 > 0.

The first option adds two areas against the axis, which is not the region between the curves; the second flips a sign that is already correct and gives a negative number; the fourth subtracts bottom minus top and is also negative.

questions.q: Find the area between the curve y = 3x − x² and the x-axis. Show your working.
questions.concept: Area between a parabola and the x-axis
questions.why:
No interval is given, so the limits are the roots: 3x − x² = x(3 − x) = 0 gives x = 0 and x = 3. Test an interior point: f(1) = 3 − 1 = 2 > 0, so the curve is above the axis on [0, 3] and no modulus is needed. A = ∫₀³(3x − x²)dx = [3x²/2 − x³/3]₀³ = (27/2 − 9) − 0 = 9/2.

Final answer: 9/2 square units (also accepted: 4.5). The working must show the roots from f(x) = 0, a sign check, and the evaluated bracket. 27/2 alone forgets the cubic term; −9/2 has the integrand upside down.

questions.q: Find the area between the curves y = x² + 1 and y = x from x = 0 to x = 2. Show your working.
questions.concept: Area between two curves on a given interval
questions.why:
Decide which curve is on top with a test point: at x = 1, x² + 1 = 2 and x = 1, so y = x² + 1 is on top (in fact x² + 1 − x = (x − 1/2)² + 3/4 > 0 everywhere, so the curves never cross). A = ∫₀²[(x² + 1) − x]dx = ∫₀²(x² − x + 1)dx = [x³/3 − x²/2 + x]₀² = 8/3 − 2 + 2 = 8/3.

Final answer: 8/3 square units (also accepted: 2.67 or 2⅔). A correct answer names the top curve, integrates top minus bottom over [0, 2] and evaluates at both limits. −8/3 comes from subtracting in the wrong order; 14/3 forgets to subtract the lower curve.

questions.q: Find the area between y = sin x and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = π. Show your working.
questions.concept: Area under a sine curve
questions.why:
sin x ≥ 0 on [0, π] (test x = π/2: sin(π/2) = 1 > 0), so A = ∫₀^π sin x dx. The antiderivative of sin x is −cos x, so A = [−cos x]₀^π = −cos π − (−cos 0) = −(−1) + 1 = 2.

Final answer: 2 square units. The working must use ∫sin x dx = −cos x, with cos π = −1 and cos 0 = 1. −2 comes from using cos x as the antiderivative, [cos x]₀^π = −1 − 1; 0 comes from taking cos π = 1 instead of −1. Neither is accepted.

questions.q: f(x) ≤ 0 for every x in [a, b]. Explain why the area between y = f(x) and the x-axis on [a, b] is |∫ₐᵇf(x)dx| and not ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx, and why that modulus is not enough if f changes sign inside [a, b].
questions.concept: Why the modulus in the area formula
questions.why:
When f ≤ 0 every strip contributes a negative amount, so ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx comes out negative (or zero); an area cannot be negative, so the area is the magnitude of the integral, |∫ₐᵇf(x)dx|. If f changes sign at some c inside [a, b], the negative contribution from one side and the positive contribution from the other cancel inside the single integral before any modulus is applied, so |∫ₐᵇf(x)dx| is smaller than the true area (it can even be 0). The remedy is to split at c and add |∫ₐᶜf(x)dx| and |∫ᶜᵇf(x)dx| separately.

A correct answer says the integral is negative below the axis, that the modulus restores a positive area, and that with a sign change the pieces cancel so the split must happen before taking magnitudes.

checks.topic:
Electromagnetic induction as concepts.

What magnetic flux is, and which angle enters Phi = B*A*cos(theta).

The three ways of changing it, and why a changing flux - not motion - is the criterion.

Why an emf appears in an open circuit with no current.

What the minus sign in emf = -N d(Phi)/dt means, and what sign convention it belongs to.

Lenz's law as opposition to the change rather than to the field, and the energy argument that forces that direction.

What self-inductance actually opposes.

questions.q: A flat coil of area 0.040 m² sits in a uniform field of 0.25 T. The plane of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the field. What is the magnetic flux through the coil?
questions.concept: Magnetic flux with the angle measured from the normal
questions.why:
Φ = BA cos θ with θ the angle between B and the normal to the coil. The plane is at 30° to B, so the normal is at 90° − 30° = 60°. Φ = (0.25)(0.040) cos 60° = (0.010)(0.50) = 5.0 × 10⁻³ Wb.

8.7 × 10⁻³ Wb uses cos 30°, taking the angle from the plane instead of the normal; 1.0 × 10⁻² Wb is BA with the angle ignored; 0.13 Wb is B cos 60° with the area left out, a field in teslas quoted as a flux.

questions.q: The flux through each turn of a 40-turn coil rises uniformly from 3.0 mWb to 9.0 mWb in 0.20 s. What is the magnitude of the induced emf?
questions.concept: Faraday's law from a flux change
questions.why:
ε = N ΔΦ/Δt. ΔΦ = 9.0 − 3.0 = 6.0 mWb = 6.0 × 10⁻³ Wb, so ε = (40)(6.0 × 10⁻³)/(0.20) = 1.2 V.

0.030 V drops N and is the emf of a single turn; 1.8 V uses the final flux 9.0 mWb instead of the change; 2.4 V adds the two fluxes (12 mWb) instead of subtracting them.

questions.q: The south pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards the face of a flat coil. Viewed from the magnet, which way does the induced current circulate, and what pole does the near face of the coil become?
options: Anticlockwise; the near face becomes a north pole
Clockwise; the near face becomes a south pole
Clockwise; the near face becomes a north pole
Anticlockwise; the near face becomes a south pole
questions.concept: Lenz's law: direction of current for an approaching pole
questions.why:
Lenz's law: the coil opposes the approach, so the near face must repel the incoming south pole by becoming a south pole itself. A face is a south pole when the current seen from that side runs clockwise (right-hand grip: clockwise current gives a field pointing away from the viewer, and field lines enter a south pole). So: clockwise, south face.

Anticlockwise with a north face is the answer for an approaching north pole, the poles swapped; clockwise with a north face pairs the right sense with the wrong pole; anticlockwise with a south face gets the grip rule backwards, and an anticlockwise current would in fact make a north face that pulls the magnet in.

questions.q: A straight rod 60 cm long moves at 5.0 m/s at right angles to both its own length and a uniform field of 0.20 T. What is the emf between the ends of the rod?
questions.concept: Motional emf of a moving rod
questions.why:
ε = BLv with L in metres: L = 60 cm = 0.60 m, so ε = (0.20)(0.60)(5.0) = 0.60 V. Unit check: T × m × m/s = V.

1.0 V is Bv with the length dropped; 0.12 V is BL with the speed dropped; 60 V leaves the length in centimetres, a factor of 100 too large.

questions.q: The current in an inductor of 0.80 H falls uniformly from 6.0 A to 2.0 A in 0.050 s. What is the magnitude of the self-induced emf?
questions.concept: Back-emf from a rate of change of current
questions.why:
|ε| = L ΔI/Δt. ΔI = 6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 A, so ΔI/Δt = 4.0/0.050 = 80 A/s and |ε| = (0.80)(80) = 64 V. Only the rate matters, not the size of the current.

96 V uses the initial 6.0 A as the change (120 A/s); 32 V uses the final 2.0 A as the change (40 A/s); 3.2 V is L ΔI with the time forgotten, which has the units of webers, not volts.

questions.q: An ideal transformer has 1200 primary turns and 60 secondary turns. The primary is connected to a 240 V a.c. supply. What is the secondary voltage?
questions.concept: Transformer voltage from the turns ratio
questions.why:
V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p, so V_s = 240 × (60/1200) = 240/20 = 12 V. Fewer secondary turns means a step-down.

4800 V inverts the turns ratio and steps up with fewer turns; 20 V is the turns ratio 1200/60 itself quoted as a voltage; 0.20 V divides 240 V by the primary turns alone and never multiplies by the secondary turns.

questions.q: A 400-turn coil carries a current of 2.0 A, and the flux through each turn is 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ Wb. What is the self-inductance of the coil?
questions.concept: Self-inductance from flux linkage
questions.why:
L = NΦ/I. Flux linkage NΦ = (400)(5.0 × 10⁻⁵) = 0.020 Wb, so L = 0.020/2.0 = 0.010 H (10 mH). Unit check: Wb/A = H.

2.5 × 10⁻⁵ H is Φ/I with N forgotten; 0.040 H multiplies NΦ by the current instead of dividing; 0.020 H is the flux linkage itself in webers, never divided by I.

questions.q: The magnetic flux through a closed loop is decreasing. Inside the loop, the field produced by the induced current points:
options: Nowhere; no current is induced because the loop is not moving
In the same direction as the applied field
questions.concept: Lenz's law opposes the change, not the field
questions.why:
Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change in flux. The flux is falling, so the induced current acts to keep it up: its own field points along the applied field, adding to it.

'Opposite to the applied field' is right only when the flux is rising; it is the half-remembered rule 'the induced field opposes B', which is wrong half the time. A perpendicular field cannot change the flux at all. Motion is not needed: a changing flux is the only criterion, so a stationary loop in a falling field does carry a current.

questions.q: An inductor of 0.60 H carries a steady current of 5.0 A. Calculate the energy stored in its magnetic field. The current is then reduced to 2.5 A. Calculate the new stored energy and state the factor by which it has fallen. Show your working.
questions.concept: Energy stored in an inductor
questions.why:
U = ½LI². At 5.0 A: U = ½(0.60)(5.0)² = ½(0.60)(25) = 7.5 J. At 2.5 A: U = ½(0.60)(2.5)² = ½(0.60)(6.25) = 1.875 J, about 1.9 J. Halving the current divides the energy by 2² = 4, because U depends on I².

Final answer: 7.5 J (accept 7.4 to 7.6) and 1.9 J (accept 1.8 to 2.0), the energy falling by a factor of 4. A correct answer shows both substitutions and states the factor 4, not 2. 15 J or 3.75 J means the ½ was dropped; 1.5 J and 0.75 J mean the current was not squared.

questions.q: A 250-turn square coil of side 4.0 cm lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.30 T. The coil is pulled completely out of the field in 0.040 s. Calculate the average emf induced in the coil. Show your working.
questions.concept: Emf from a coil removed from a field
questions.why:
Area in SI: A = (0.040)² = 1.6 × 10⁻³ m². Plane perpendicular to B means the normal is along B, so θ = 0 and the initial flux per turn is Φ = BA = (0.30)(1.6 × 10⁻³) = 4.8 × 10⁻⁴ Wb; the final flux is zero, so ΔΦ = 4.8 × 10⁻⁴ Wb. ε = N ΔΦ/Δt = (250)(4.8 × 10⁻⁴)/(0.040) = 0.12/0.040 = 3.0 V.

Final answer: 3.0 V (accept 2.9 to 3.1). A correct answer converts the side to metres, uses the full flux as the change (the coil leaves the field entirely), multiplies by N and divides by the time. 0.012 V forgot N; 3.0 × 10⁴ V left the side in centimetres; 0 V wrongly took 'plane perpendicular to B' to mean no flux.

questions.q: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.15 H. The current in the first coil falls uniformly from 6.0 A to zero in 0.030 s. Calculate the emf induced in the second coil during the change, and state the emf in the second coil while the 6.0 A was held steady. Show your working.
questions.concept: Mutually induced emf from a current change
questions.why:
ε₂ = M ΔI₁/Δt. ΔI₁/Δt = 6.0/0.030 = 200 A/s, so ε₂ = (0.15)(200) = 30 V. While the current was held steady, ΔI₁/Δt = 0, so the induced emf in the second coil was zero, however large the steady current.

Final answer: 30 V (accept 29 to 31) during the change, and 0 V while steady. A correct answer computes the rate 200 A/s, multiplies by M, and states that a steady current induces nothing. 0.90 V is M × ΔI with the time forgotten; 200 V is the rate 200 A/s quoted as a voltage with M left out; both are wrong.

questions.q: A hand-cranked generator turns freely when its output terminals are left open, but becomes noticeably harder to turn the moment a lamp is connected across them. Explain why, using Lenz's law and conservation of energy.
questions.concept: Lenz's law as conservation of energy
questions.why:
With the terminals open an emf is induced in the rotating coil but no current flows, so the coil carries no current and feels no magnetic force; only friction resists the crank. Connect the lamp and a current flows in the coil, which sits in the machine's field, so there is a force (torque) on it. By Lenz's law that torque opposes the rotation producing it, so the crank fights back.

Conservation of energy demands this: the lamp dissipates electrical energy, and the only source is the work done by the hand. If the induced current instead helped the rotation, the generator would speed up on its own while also lighting the lamp, energy from nothing. A correct answer states (1) no current so no force when open, (2) current in a field gives a torque that opposes the motion by Lenz's law, and (3) the extra effort is the mechanical work that becomes the lamp's electrical energy.

checks.topic:
Arrays and recursion as concepts.

The course's definition of an array, and what each of 'fixed-size', 'sequential collection' and 'elements of the same type' makes possible.

The declaration syntax datatype arrayName[arraySize], and the one-sided initialiser rule.

Why an index is an offset, so that the first is 0 and the largest for int a[10] is 9. What happens at compile time and at run time when an index falls outside that range.

The two components a recursive function must have. Plus the implicit third condition: every call must make progress that actually lands on the base case.

The call stack, with one frame and one set of parameters per call, and its pending operations.

Direct versus indirect, and tail versus non-tail recursion, as two independent classifications.

What the deck's iteration-versus-recursion table really trades away.

questions.q: `int a[10];` is stored as one block starting at address 1000, and each int occupies 4 bytes. At what address does `a[7]` start?
questions.concept: Index as an offset
questions.why:
An index is an offset from the first element: a[i] starts at start + i × width. So a[7] starts at 1000 + 7 × 4 = 1028.

1032 is 1000 + 8 × 4, counting a[7] as the eighth element and using 8 as the offset; 1007 adds the index without multiplying by the 4-byte width; 1024 is 1000 + 6 × 4, one element short.

questions.q: After `int v[6] = {3, 8, 1};` the statement `int x = v[1] + v[3];` runs. What is x?
options: Unpredictable, because v[3] was never given a value
questions.concept: Partial initialiser and zero filling
questions.why:
Fewer values than elements is legal, and the elements not listed become 0. So v[0] = 3, v[1] = 8, v[2] = 1, v[3] = v[4] = v[5] = 0. Indexing is zero-based, so x = v[1] + v[3] = 8 + 0 = 8.

4 reads the indices one-based (v[1] as 3, v[3] as 1); 9 takes v[1] = 8 but reads v[3] as the third value, 1; the last option treats an unlisted element as garbage, which is true only for an array with no initialiser at all.

questions.concept: Row and column subscripts
questions.why:
The first subscript is the row and the second is the column, both counted from 0. m[2][0] is row 2, column 0, which is 7; m[0][1] is row 0, column 1, which is 2. Sum: 9.

7 transposes the subscripts, reading m[0][2] + m[1][0] = 3 + 4; 11 reads the columns one-based, m[2][1] + m[0][2] = 8 + 3; 5 reads the rows one-based, m[1][0] + m[0][0] = 4 + 1.

questions.q: Exactly one of these declarations is rejected by the compiler. Which?
questions.concept: One-sided initialiser rule
questions.why:
The number of values between the braces cannot be larger than the number of elements declared between the square brackets. p declares 3 elements and is handed 4, so it is rejected.

q is legal: fewer values is allowed and the rest become 0, giving {1, 0, 0}. r is legal: with the size omitted, an array just big enough for the initialiser is created, size 2. s matches exactly. Believing q is illegal reads the rule as two-sided; believing r is illegal forgets that the size may be inferred.

questions.concept: Counting recursive calls
questions.why:
Each call subtracts 2: g(9) calls g(7), which calls g(5), then g(3), then g(1). g(1) satisfies n <= 1 and returns without calling again. That is 5 calls, all alive at once because each is waiting for the one below it: 5 frames.

4 counts only the recursive calls and forgets the original g(9) frame; 9 assumes the argument steps down by 1; 'never terminates' misreads n <= 1 as n == 0, which 9 would indeed step over.

questions.concept: Reachability of the base case
questions.why:
The base case is n == 0 and each call subtracts 3, so the call lands exactly on 0 only when n is a multiple of 3. h(9): 9, 6, 3, 0 terminates. h(12): 12, 9, 6, 3, 0 terminates. h(10) goes 10, 7, 4, 1, −2, −5, ... and h(7) goes 7, 4, 1, −2, ... stepping straight over 0 and never stopping.

'All four' assumes having a base case is enough, without checking that the calls reach it; 'h(9) only' and 'h(12) only' each miss that the other is also a multiple of 3.

questions.concept: Tracing an accumulator parameter
questions.why:
The product is carried down in acc: p(4, 1) calls p(3, 4), then p(2, 12), then p(1, 24), then p(0, 24). At n = 0 the base case returns acc = 24, and since nothing is pending in any frame, 24 is passed back unchanged.

10 adds n to acc instead of multiplying (4 + 3 + 2 + 1); 0 multiplies by n before testing the base case, so the final step is 24 × 0; 1 returns the starting acc, forgetting that each call replaces it.

questions.q: `isEven(n)` returns 1 if n is 0 and otherwise returns `isOdd(n − 1)`; `isOdd(n)` returns 0 if n is 0 and otherwise returns `isEven(n − 1)`. Neither function names itself. How is this classified?
options: Not recursion, since neither function calls itself
questions.concept: Direct versus indirect recursion
questions.why:
Indirect recursion is when a function contains a call to another function which eventually calls the function back. isEven calls isOdd, which calls isEven again, so isEven does reach itself, just through a second function. Recursion covers a function that calls itself indirectly as well as directly.

Direct recursion needs an explicit call to itself, which neither has; 'not recursion' drops the word indirectly from the definition; iteration would be a loop inside one call, with no new frame per step.

questions.concept: Call stack of a non-tail recursion
questions.why:
Descending: f(3) needs f(2) and has + 9 pending; f(2) needs f(1) and has + 4 pending; f(1) needs f(0) and has + 1 pending; f(0) is the base case and returns 0 with nothing pending. Four frames are alive at the deepest point. Ascending: f(1) = 0 + 1 = 1; f(2) = 1 + 4 = 5; f(3) = 5 + 9 = 14.

Final answer: 14. A correct answer lists the four calls f(3), f(2), f(1), f(0) in that order, names the pending addition of n² in each of the first three frames, and gives the returns 0, 1, 5, 14 in ascending order. Giving 9 (only the top frame's term) or 6 (forgetting the squares) is wrong.

questions.q: `int a[4] = {7, 3, 9, 12};` State the largest legal index and the value of `a[3]`. Then say exactly what happens at compile time and at run time when the statement `a[4] = 0;` is executed, and why. Show your working.
questions.concept: Out-of-range index behaviour
questions.why:
The declaration reserves a block of 4 ints at offsets 0, 1, 2, 3, so the largest legal index is 3 and a[3] is the fourth value, 12. a[4] names the location one past the end of the block. At compile time nothing happens: the statement is valid C and builds without a warning. At run time nothing is checked either, because no length is stored and a[4] is simply computed as start + 4 × width. The 0 is therefore written into memory belonging to something else, which is undefined behaviour: a neighbouring variable may be corrupted, the program may print a wrong answer, or it may crash, and the symptom can differ between runs.

A correct answer states index 3, value 12, that the code compiles, that no run-time check exists, and that the write lands outside the array with unpredictable effect. Saying the compiler rejects it, or that the array grows to 5 elements, is wrong.

questions.concept: Bounds of a two-dimensional traversal
questions.why:
m has 2 rows (i = 0, 1) and 3 columns (j = 0, 1, 2), but the loop limits are swapped. It accesses m[0][0], m[0][1], m[1][0], m[1][1], m[2][0], m[2][1]. The last two are out of range: there is no row 2, and nothing reports it, so junk is added to t. The elements m[0][2] and m[1][2] (values 3 and 6) are never visited. The corrected loop is `for (i = 0; i < 2; i++) for (j = 0; j < 3; j++) t = t + m[i][j];`, which gives t = 21.

A correct answer lists the six accesses, names m[2][0] and m[2][1] as out of range, names m[0][2] and m[1][2] as missed, and puts the row count 2 on the outer loop and the column count 3 on the inner one. Also accepted: i <= 1 and j <= 2 as the conditions.

questions.q: The recursive factorial declares no local variables and is a single return statement, yet at run time it uses more memory than the loop with its two variables i and result. Explain where that memory goes and what it means to say the computer does more work while the programmer does less.
questions.concept: Iteration versus recursion
questions.why:
Every call gets its own stack frame holding its own copy of n and a note of where to resume. factorial(n) cannot multiply until factorial(n − 1) returns, so its frame stays alive with a multiplication pending, and so on down: at the deepest point n frames exist and n − 1 multiplications are waiting. The loop keeps everything in one frame and overwrites result each pass, so its memory does not grow with n. The programmer does less because there is no counter to start, no accumulator to seed and no loop condition to get wrong; the computer does more because it creates and tears down n frames and holds them all at once, which is slower and can overflow the stack for large n.

A correct answer mentions one frame per call with its own n, the pending operation kept in each frame, memory growing with n versus constant for the loop, and names what the programmer is spared.

checks.topic:
Problems-only session on Week 10.

Compute areas between a curve and the x-axis, with limits found from f(x) = 0: ∫₀⁵(5x − x²)dx, and the split case for x² − 1 on [0, 2].

Compute areas between two curves, with limits from f(x) = g(x): y = 3 − x with y = x² − 9, and 2 − x with 4 − x².

Then across an interior crossing, using A = A₁ + A₂.

Includes all three TASKs the lecturer set and never answered: 6x − x² against the axis; y = x² with y = 2 − x² on [0, 2]; and y = cos x with y = 2 − cos x on [0, 2π].

questions.q: Find the area between the curve y = x² − 3x and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 4.
questions.concept: Area against the axis with a split at a root
questions.why:
x² − 3x = x(x − 3) is zero at x = 3, inside [0, 4]; f ≤ 0 on [0, 3] and f ≥ 0 on [3, 4]. With F(x) = x³/3 − 3x²/2: |F(3) − F(0)| = |9 − 27/2| = 9/2 and F(4) − F(3) = (64/3 − 24) − (−9/2) = −8/3 + 9/2 = 11/6. A = 9/2 + 11/6 = 27/6 + 11/6 = 38/6 = 19/3 square units.

9/2 is the piece below the axis only; 11/6 is the piece above only; 8/3 is the magnitude of the unsplit integral ∫₀⁴(x² − 3x)dx = −8/3, in which the pieces cancel.

questions.q: Find the area of the region enclosed by the line y = x + 4 and the parabola y = x² − 2x.
questions.concept: Area enclosed by a line and a parabola
questions.why:
Limits: x + 4 = x² − 2x gives x² − 3x − 4 = (x − 4)(x + 1) = 0, so x = −1 and x = 4. At x = 0 the line gives 4 and the parabola 0, so the line is on top. A = ∫₋₁⁴[(x + 4) − (x² − 2x)]dx = ∫₋₁⁴(3x + 4 − x²)dx = [3x²/2 + 4x − x³/3]₋₁⁴ = 56/3 − (−13/6) = 112/6 + 13/6 = 125/6 square units.

56/3 is the value at the upper limit alone; −125/6 subtracts parabola minus line, the wrong order; 33/2 is 56/3 − 13/6, from failing to double the minus when subtracting the negative lower-limit value.

questions.q: Find the area of the region enclosed by the parabolas y = x² and y = 8 − x².
questions.concept: Area enclosed by two parabolas
questions.why:
Limits: x² = 8 − x² gives x² = 4, so x = −2 and x = 2. At x = 0, 8 − x² = 8 is above x² = 0, so A = ∫₋₂²[(8 − x²) − x²]dx = ∫₋₂²(8 − 2x²)dx = [8x − 2x³/3]₋₂² = (16 − 16/3) − (−16 + 16/3) = 32 − 32/3 = 64/3 square units.

32/3 integrates from 0 to 2 only and forgets the left half; 80/3 is ∫₋₂²(8 − x²)dx, the area under the top curve with the lower curve never subtracted; −64/3 subtracts in the wrong order.

questions.q: Find the total area between the curves y = x³ and y = x from x = 0 to x = 2.
questions.concept: Area between curves that cross inside the interval
questions.why:
x³ = x gives x(x² − 1) = 0, so the curves cross at x = 1 inside [0, 2]. On [0, 1] the line is on top (at x = 1/2: 1/2 > 1/8); on [1, 2] the cubic is on top (at x = 2: 8 > 2). A₁ = ∫₀¹(x − x³)dx = 1/2 − 1/4 = 1/4 and A₂ = ∫₁²(x³ − x)dx = (4 − 2) − (1/4 − 1/2) = 9/4. A = 1/4 + 9/4 = 10/4 = 5/2 square units.

9/4 is the second piece only; 2 is the magnitude of the single integral ∫₀²(x − x³)dx = 2 − 4 = −2, where the pieces cancel; 1/4 is the first piece only.

questions.q: Find the area between the curves y = cos x and y = 3 − cos x from x = 0 to x = π.
questions.concept: Area between trigonometric curves without a crossing
questions.why:
Check for crossings: cos x = 3 − cos x gives cos x = 3/2, impossible, so the curves never meet and one integral suffices. At x = 0: 3 − cos 0 = 2 > cos 0 = 1, so y = 3 − cos x is on top throughout. A = ∫₀^π[(3 − cos x) − cos x]dx = ∫₀^π(3 − 2cos x)dx = [3x − 2sin x]₀^π = (3π − 0) − (0 − 0) = 3π square units.

3π − 4 integrates cos x to −cos x (the antiderivative of sin x), giving [3x + 2cos x]₀^π = (3π − 2) − 2; 6π integrates over [0, 2π] instead of the given [0, π]; −3π subtracts in the wrong order.

questions.q: The area between the curve y = x² and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = a (with a > 0) is 9 square units. Find a.
questions.concept: Finding a limit from a given area
questions.why:
x² ≥ 0, so A = ∫₀ᵃx²dx = [x³/3]₀ᵃ = a³/3. Set a³/3 = 9, so a³ = 27 and a = 3. Check: ∫₀³x²dx = 27/3 = 9.

a = 27 stops at a³ = 27 without taking the cube root; a = ∛9 forgets to multiply by 3 and solves a³ = 9; a = 3√2 integrates x instead of x², solving a²/2 = 9.

questions.q: Find the area between the curve y = x² − 2x − 8 and the x-axis from x = −1 to x = 3.
questions.concept: Area below the axis on an interval with a negative lower limit
questions.why:
Roots: x² − 2x − 8 = (x − 4)(x + 2) = 0 gives x = −2 and x = 4, both outside [−1, 3], so f does not change sign there; f(0) = −8 < 0, so the curve is below the axis on the whole interval and A = |∫₋₁³(x² − 2x − 8)dx|. With F(x) = x³/3 − x² − 8x: F(3) = 9 − 9 − 24 = −24 and F(−1) = −1/3 − 1 + 8 = 20/3, so the integral is −24 − 20/3 = −92/3 and A = 92/3 square units.

52/3 evaluates F(−1) with the wrong sign, giving −24 + 20/3; −92/3 forgets the modulus and reports a negative area; 24 is the upper-limit value alone.

questions.q: Two curves y = f(x) and y = g(x) cross once at x = c inside [a, b]. A₁ = ∫ₐᶜ(f(x) − g(x))dx > 0 and A₂ = ∫ᶜᵇ(g(x) − f(x))dx > 0. What is the single integral ∫ₐᵇ(f(x) − g(x))dx equal to?
questions.concept: What a single integral across a crossing computes
questions.why:
Integrals add over adjacent intervals: ∫ₐᵇ(f − g)dx = ∫ₐᶜ(f − g)dx + ∫ᶜᵇ(f − g)dx = A₁ + (−A₂) = A₁ − A₂, because on [c, b] the integrand f − g is the negative of g − f. The true area is A₁ + A₂, so the single integral undercounts by 2A₂.

A₁ + A₂ is the area, not the single integral; 0 happens only in the special case A₁ = A₂ (as for sin x and cos x on [0, π/2]); |A₁ − A₂| is the modulus of the single integral, which still is not the area.

questions.q: Find the total area between the curves y = sin x and y = cos x from x = 0 to x = π. Show your working.
questions.concept: Area between sine and cosine across a crossing
questions.why:
Crossing: sin x = cos x gives tan x = 1, so x = π/4 in [0, π]. On [0, π/4] cos x is on top (at x = 0: 1 > 0); on [π/4, π] sin x is on top (at x = π/2: 1 > 0). A₁ = ∫₀^(π/4)(cos x − sin x)dx = [sin x + cos x]₀^(π/4) = (1/√2 + 1/√2) − (0 + 1) = √2 − 1. A₂ = ∫_(π/4)^π(sin x − cos x)dx = [−cos x − sin x]_(π/4)^π = (1 − 0) − (−1/√2 − 1/√2) = 1 + √2. A = A₁ + A₂ = 2√2.

Final answer: 2√2 square units (also accepted: 4/√2, or 2.83 to two decimal places). The working must find the crossing at π/4, split there with the top function first in each piece, and add. A single integral ∫₀^π(cos x − sin x)dx = 2 − 2√2 is negative and is not accepted; √2 − 1 alone is only the first piece.

questions.q: Find the total area of the region enclosed by the curve y = x³ and the line y = 4x. Show your working.
questions.concept: Area enclosed by a cubic and a line through the origin
questions.why:
Intersections: x³ = 4x gives x(x² − 4) = 0, so x = −2, 0, 2. The region has two lobes and the curves cross at x = 0, so split there. On [−2, 0] the cubic is on top (at x = −1: −1 > −4); on [0, 2] the line is on top (at x = 1: 4 > 1). A₁ = ∫₋₂⁰(x³ − 4x)dx = [x⁴/4 − 2x²]₋₂⁰ = 0 − (4 − 8) = 4. A₂ = ∫₀²(4x − x³)dx = [2x² − x⁴/4]₀² = 8 − 4 = 4. A = 4 + 4 = 8.

Final answer: 8 square units. Using the symmetry of the two lobes, A = 2 × 4 = 8, is also accepted, provided one lobe is integrated correctly. A single integral ∫₋₂²(4x − x³)dx = 0 is wrong because the lobes cancel; 4 alone is one lobe.

questions.q: Find the area of the region enclosed by the curve y = x³ − 6x² + 9x and the x-axis. Show your working.
questions.concept: Area between a cubic and the x-axis with a repeated root
questions.why:
Limits from f(x) = 0: x³ − 6x² + 9x = x(x² − 6x + 9) = x(x − 3)², so the curve meets the axis at x = 0 and x = 3 (a double root, where the curve touches without crossing). The enclosed region is on [0, 3]; test x = 1: 1 − 6 + 9 = 4 > 0, so the curve is above the axis there and no modulus is needed. A = ∫₀³(x³ − 6x² + 9x)dx = [x⁴/4 − 2x³ + 9x²/2]₀³ = 81/4 − 54 + 81/2 = (81 − 216 + 162)/4 = 27/4.

Final answer: 27/4 square units (also accepted: 6.75). The working must factorise to find the roots 0 and 3, include a sign check, and evaluate the bracket at both limits. Splitting at x = 3 changes nothing because the curve does not cross there; −27/4 has a sign error in the evaluation.

questions.q: Both y = f(x) and y = g(x) cross the x-axis somewhere inside [a, b], but f(x) ≥ g(x) for every x in [a, b]. Explain whether the integral for the area between the two curves must be split into pieces, and why.
questions.concept: When a split is needed for two curves
questions.why:
No split is needed. The height of a vertical strip between the curves is f(x) − g(x), a difference of y-values, and it stays non-negative on the whole of [a, b] because f is on top throughout. Where either curve crosses the x-axis is irrelevant: the axis is not one of the boundaries of the region. So A = ∫ₐᵇ(f(x) − g(x))dx in one piece. Splitting is required only where the two curves cross each other, that is where f(x) = g(x) inside (a, b), because there the integrand changes sign and the pieces would cancel.

A correct answer says one integral of f − g is enough, that the strip height ignores the x-axis, and that the split point for two curves is a solution of f(x) = g(x), not of f(x) = 0 or g(x) = 0.

checks.topic:
Numerical induction work.

Computing Phi = B*A*cos(theta), with areas and angles converted properly.

emf = N*d(Phi)/dt, and the induced charge q = N*d(Phi)/R.

Motional emf = B*L*v, with the retarding force B^2*L^2*v/R and the mechanical-to-electrical power audit.

The rotating-coil peak emf = N*B*A*omega, with the 2*pi*f and rms traps.

Self-inductance L = mu_0*mu_r*N^2*A/l, with back-emf L*dI/dt and stored energy 0.5*L*I^2.

Then mutual inductance, and the ideal transformer's turns and current ratios.

questions.q: A circular coil of 150 turns has a diameter of 8.0 cm. Its plane is perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.50 T. What is the flux linkage NΦ of the coil?
questions.concept: Flux linkage of a circular coil
questions.why:
Radius r = 4.0 cm = 0.040 m, so A = πr² = π(0.040)² = 5.03 × 10⁻³ m². Plane perpendicular to B means θ = 0, so Φ = BA = (0.50)(5.03 × 10⁻³) = 2.51 × 10⁻³ Wb per turn, and NΦ = 150 × 2.51 × 10⁻³ = 0.377 Wb, about 0.38 Wb.

1.5 Wb uses the diameter 0.080 m as the radius, four times too much area; 2.5 × 10⁻³ Wb is the flux through one turn with N forgotten; 0 Wb misreads 'plane perpendicular to B' as θ = 90°, when the normal is in fact along B.

questions.q: A 200-turn coil of area 3.0 × 10⁻³ m² and total resistance 4.0 Ω has its plane perpendicular to a uniform field. The field falls from 0.80 T to 0.20 T in 0.50 s. How much charge flows round the circuit during the change?
questions.concept: Induced charge through a coil
questions.why:
q = N ΔΦ/R, and the time does not enter. ΔΦ = ΔB × A = (0.80 − 0.20)(3.0 × 10⁻³) = 1.8 × 10⁻³ Wb; N ΔΦ = 0.36 Wb; q = 0.36/4.0 = 0.090 C.

0.18 C is the current (ε = 0.72 V, I = 0.18 A) reported as a charge, the 0.50 s divided in and never multiplied back out; 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ C forgets N; 0.030 C uses the final field 0.20 T instead of the change 0.60 T.

questions.q: A rod of length 0.40 m slides at 3.0 m/s on rails in a field of 0.50 T perpendicular to the plane of the circuit. The total resistance is 0.20 Ω. What is the magnitude of the magnetic force on the rod?
questions.concept: Retarding force on a rod moving in a field
questions.why:
Chain three formulas: ε = BLv = (0.50)(0.40)(3.0) = 0.60 V; I = ε/R = 0.60/0.20 = 3.0 A; F = BIL = (0.50)(3.0)(0.40) = 0.60 N, directed against the motion. Equivalently F = B²L²v/R = (0.25)(0.16)(3.0)/0.20 = 0.60 N.

0.12 N uses the emf 0.60 V as if it were the current, never dividing by R; 1.2 N is BL²v/R, with B not squared; 1.5 N is B²Lv/R, with L not squared.

questions.q: A coil of 100 turns and area 80 cm² rotates at 25 revolutions per second in a uniform field of 0.12 T, about an axis perpendicular to the field. What is the peak emf?
questions.concept: Peak emf of a rotating coil
questions.why:
ε₀ = NBAω. A = 80 cm² = 80 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.0 × 10⁻³ m²; ω = 2πf = 2π(25) = 157 rad/s. ε₀ = (100)(0.12)(8.0 × 10⁻³)(157) = 15.1 V, about 15 V.

2.4 V uses f = 25 in place of ω, missing the factor 2π; 11 V is the rms value ε₀/√2, not the peak; 1.5 × 10³ V converts cm² with 10⁻² instead of 10⁻⁴.

questions.q: An air-cored solenoid has a self-inductance of 2.0 mH. Its number of turns is doubled with the length and area unchanged, and an iron core of relative permeability 200 is inserted. What is the new inductance?
questions.concept: Scaling of solenoid inductance with turns and core
questions.why:
L = μ₀μᵣN²A/ℓ. Doubling N multiplies L by 2² = 4; the core multiplies it by μᵣ = 200. New L = 2.0 mH × 4 × 200 = 1600 mH = 1.6 H.

0.80 H scales with N instead of N², a factor 2 for the turns; 8.0 mH applies the N² factor but forgets the core; 0.40 H applies the core but forgets the extra turns.

questions.q: A solenoid of 600 turns, length 0.25 m and cross-sectional area 4.0 cm² has a 200-turn coil wound tightly over its middle. The core is air, μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. What is the mutual inductance of the pair?
questions.concept: Mutual inductance of coaxial coils
questions.why:
M = μ₀N₁N₂A/ℓ with A = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²: M = (4π × 10⁻⁷)(600)(200)(4.0 × 10⁻⁴)/(0.25) = (1.257 × 10⁻⁶)(1.2 × 10⁵)(1.6 × 10⁻³) = 2.41 × 10⁻⁴ H, about 0.24 mH.

7.2 × 10⁻⁴ H uses 600² in place of 600 × 200 and is the self-inductance of the solenoid; 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ H uses 200²; 2.4 × 10⁻² H converts cm² with 10⁻² instead of 10⁻⁴.

questions.q: An ideal transformer steps 240 V a.c. down to 12 V. The secondary drives a lamp of resistance 4.0 Ω. What current does the primary draw?
questions.concept: Primary current of a loaded transformer
questions.why:
Secondary current I_s = V_s/R = 12/4.0 = 3.0 A; secondary power = V_sI_s = 36 W. Ideal, so primary power is the same: I_p = 36/240 = 0.15 A. Check: the voltage is stepped down by 20, so the current is stepped up by 20, and 3.0/20 = 0.15 A.

3.0 A assumes the same current on both sides, which would mean the primary takes 720 W to deliver 36 W; 60 A inverts the ratio and multiplies 3.0 A by 20; 0.60 A divides 12 V by the turns ratio 20, a voltage treated as a current.

questions.q: The rotation rate of a generator coil in a fixed field is doubled. What happens to the peak emf and to the frequency of the output?
questions.concept: Dependence of generator output on rotation rate
questions.why:
ε₀ = NBAω and f = ω/2π. Doubling the rotation rate doubles ω, so the peak emf doubles and the output frequency doubles, one cycle per revolution.

'Frequency unchanged' forgets that each revolution is one cycle; 'both quadruple' squares a linear dependence; 'peak emf quadruples' confuses the emf with the power into a fixed resistor, which does go up four-fold since P ∝ ε₀².

questions.q: A 60-turn circular coil, radius 5.0 cm, resistance 3.0 Ω, lies face-on to a uniform field into the page that rises uniformly from zero to 0.90 T in 0.30 s. Calculate the emf and the current, and state whether the current is clockwise or anticlockwise as seen by the reader. Show your working.
questions.concept: Faraday's law chained with Ohm's law and Lenz's law
questions.why:
A = πr² = π(0.050)² = 7.85 × 10⁻³ m². ΔΦ = ΔB × A = (0.90)(7.85 × 10⁻³) = 7.07 × 10⁻³ Wb per turn; N ΔΦ = 60 × 7.07 × 10⁻³ = 0.424 Wb. ε = N ΔΦ/Δt = 0.424/0.30 = 1.41 V. I = ε/R = 1.41/3.0 = 0.47 A. Direction: the into-page flux is increasing, so the induced current must make an out-of-page field inside the loop; by the right-hand grip rule that is an anticlockwise current as seen by the reader.

Final answer: ε = 1.4 V (accept 1.3 to 1.5), I = 0.47 A (accept 0.45 to 0.49), anticlockwise. A correct answer converts the radius to metres, multiplies by N, divides by the time, applies Ohm's law, and gives anticlockwise with the reason that the induced field opposes the growth of into-page flux. Clockwise is the answer for a decreasing field and is wrong here; 0.024 V forgot N.

questions.q: A 0.50 m rod slides at a steady 8.0 m/s on frictionless rails in a 0.30 T field perpendicular to the circuit; total resistance 0.60 Ω. Calculate the emf, the current and the mechanical power needed to keep the rod moving, and show that it equals the electrical power dissipated. Show your working.
questions.concept: Power audit of a moving rod
questions.why:
ε = BLv = (0.30)(0.50)(8.0) = 1.2 V. I = ε/R = 1.2/0.60 = 2.0 A. The retarding force is F = BIL = (0.30)(2.0)(0.50) = 0.30 N, so the mechanical power needed is P = Fv = (0.30)(8.0) = 2.4 W. Electrical power dissipated: I²R = (2.0)²(0.60) = 2.4 W, and εI = (1.2)(2.0) = 2.4 W. The two agree: the hand's work is what heats the resistor.

Final answer: 1.2 V, 2.0 A, 2.4 W mechanical = 2.4 W electrical (accept 2.3 to 2.5 W). A correct answer must compute the force (or use P = εI) and show the two powers equal. 0.30 W is the force quoted as a power; 4.8 W or 9.6 W has an extra factor of v or of I.

questions.q: An air-cored solenoid has 800 turns, length 0.20 m and area 3.0 cm²; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A. Calculate (a) its self-inductance, (b) the back-emf when the current rises uniformly from zero to 3.0 A in 15 ms, (c) the energy stored at 3.0 A. Show your working.
questions.concept: Solenoid inductance, back-emf and stored energy
questions.why:
(a) L = μ₀N²A/ℓ = (4π × 10⁻⁷)(800)²(3.0 × 10⁻⁴)/(0.20) = (1.257 × 10⁻⁶)(6.4 × 10⁵)(1.5 × 10⁻³) = 1.21 × 10⁻³ H, about 1.2 mH. (b) ΔI/Δt = 3.0/0.015 = 200 A/s, so |ε| = L ΔI/Δt = (1.21 × 10⁻³)(200) = 0.24 V. (c) U = ½LI² = ½(1.21 × 10⁻³)(3.0)² = 5.4 × 10⁻³ J, about 5.4 mJ.

Final answer: L = 1.2 mH (accept 1.15 to 1.25 mH), ε = 0.24 V (accept 0.23 to 0.25), U = 5.4 mJ (accept 5.2 to 5.6). A correct answer converts cm² to 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², squares N, and uses the rate 200 A/s rather than the current 3.0 A in (b). 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ H used N instead of N²; 0.12 H converted the area with 10⁻²; 3.6 mJ is LI, with the ½ and the square both dropped.

questions.q: A transformer is connected by mistake to a 12 V d.c. supply instead of 12 V a.c. Explain why the secondary gives no steady output, and why the primary winding is likely to overheat.
questions.concept: Why a transformer needs alternating current
questions.why:
The secondary emf is ε = −N_s dΦ/dt: it needs a changing flux in the core. A steady direct current gives a steady core flux, so after the brief switch-on transient dΦ/dt = 0 and the secondary voltage is zero. A d.c. current still makes a perfectly good field; it simply makes a constant one, and constant flux induces nothing.

The primary overheats because on a.c. the current is limited mainly by the back-emf L dI/dt of the winding; on d.c. there is no changing current and hence no back-emf, so the current is limited only by the winding's small resistance, I = V/R, which is far larger than the design current and dissipates I²R as heat. A correct answer says (1) no changing flux so no induced emf, and (2) no back-emf so a large resistive current in the primary.

checks.topic:
Code work on arrays and recursion.

Tracing a recursive call down to its base case and back up through its pending operations.

Predicting the return value of an array recursion, and the output of one- and two-dimensional array loops.

Spotting a missing base case, and a base case that is never reached.

Finding off-by-one and out-of-bounds faults in traversals and in recursive index expressions.

Distinguishing tail from non-tail recursion on a real listing.

Recognising that an array name cannot be assigned, so a copy must be a loop.

Diagnosing infinite recursion as a stack overflow rather than a hang.

questions.concept: Output order around a recursive call
questions.why:
The printf comes after the recursive call, so nothing is printed on the way down: show(3) calls show(2), which calls show(1), which calls show(0), which returns at once. Then control comes back to the point just after each call, so the prints run in reverse order of the calls: 1, then 2, then 3. Output: 1 2 3.

3 2 1 is what you get if the printf were before the call; 0 1 2 3 and 3 2 1 0 have the base case printing, but show(0) returns before reaching printf.

questions.concept: Return value of an array recursion
questions.why:
(a[n − 1] > 4) is 1 when the element is greater than 4 and 0 otherwise, so r counts the elements of a[0..n−1] that exceed 4. Unwinding: r(a, 6) adds a[5] = 1 (0), a[4] = 5 (1), a[3] = 4 (0), a[2] = 9 (1), a[1] = 2 (0), a[0] = 7 (1), on top of r(a, 0) = 0. Total 3.

21 adds the qualifying values 7 + 9 + 5 instead of counting them; 4 counts 4 itself, reading > as >=; 2 forgets that the last call, r(a, 1), examines a[0].

questions.concept: Completing a recursive case
questions.why:
The recursive case must count this digit and hand a smaller number of the same kind to the same function. n / 10 drops the last digit, so 1 + digits(n / 10) counts one digit per call: digits(4725) = 1 + digits(472) = 2 + digits(47) = 3 + digits(4) = 4.

digits(n / 10) drops the last digit but never counts it, so it returns 1 for every n; 1 + digits(n % 10) passes the last digit, which is always below 10, so it returns 2 for every n >= 10; 1 + digits(n − 10) subtracts 10 each call and counts tens, giving 473 for 4725.

questions.concept: Off-by-one in a recursive index
questions.why:
With n elements, the last one sits at offset n − 1, not n. As written, total(a, 4) adds a[4], a[3], a[2], a[1]: it reads one element past the end and never adds a[0]. Changing a[n] to a[n − 1] makes each call pick up the element at the end of its own prefix, and total(a, 1) adds a[0].

Changing the base case to n == 1 makes total(a, 0) recurse forever; changing n − 1 to n removes all progress toward the base case; changing return 0 to return a[0] adds a[0] to a sum that still reads a[n] out of range.

questions.q: `int a[n]` is filled and `int b[n]` is declared. Which statement correctly copies the contents of a into b?
questions.concept: Copying an array
questions.why:
An array name is not a modifiable value, so a copy must be made element by element with the standard traversal: start at 0, continue while i < n, step by 1, assigning each a[i] to b[i].

b = a; does not compile, because arrays cannot be assigned as a whole; the loop from 1 to n skips a[0] and writes b[n], one past the end; the last loop copies in the wrong direction, overwriting a with the unset contents of b.

questions.q: Which of these functions is tail recursive?
options: `int f(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; return f(n - 1) + 1; }`
`int h(int n) { if (n == 0) return 1; return 2 * h(n - 1); }`
`void k(int n) { if (n == 0) return; k(n - 1); printf("%d ", n); }`
`int m(int n, int b) { if (n == 0) return b; return m(n - 1, b + 2); }`
questions.concept: Tail versus non-tail recursion
questions.why:
Tail recursion means no pending operation when the recursive call returns. In m, the value of m(n − 1, b + 2) is returned unchanged; all the work was done in the argument before the call, so nothing waits. That is tail recursion.

f has + 1 waiting on the returned value; h has 2 × waiting; both have the call on the last line, which is not the test. k has a printf that runs after the call returns, so an operation is pending even though no value is combined.

questions.concept: Tracing nested array loops
questions.why:
The inner loop starts at j = i. Row 0: j = 0, 1, 2 adds 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Row 1: j = 1, 2 adds 5 + 6 = 11. t = 17.

21 ignores the start j = i and adds every element; 11 starts j at i + 1 (2 + 3 + 6); 8 uses 2 as the inner bound instead of 3 (1 + 2 + 5).

questions.q: `fact(n)` is written as `return n * fact(n - 1);` with no other line. Calling `fact(5)` ends within a second with a segmentation fault. Which diagnosis is right?
options: Stack overflow: no base case, so a new frame is added on every call until the stack runs out
Infinite loop: the program should have hung rather than stopped
Integer overflow: n became too large for an int
Compile error: the function was never built
questions.concept: Infinite recursion and the stack
questions.why:
Without a base case, fact(5) calls fact(4), fact(3), ... and keeps going past 0 into negatives. Each call is a new stack frame with a pending multiplication, so memory grows by one frame per call until the stack space is exhausted and the program is killed: a stack overflow. It fails on space, and quickly.

An infinite loop runs in constant memory and would hang, not crash; n is getting smaller, not larger, so int overflow is not the cause; the code is valid C and compiles without complaint.

questions.q: Write a recursive C function `int pw(int b, int e)` that returns b raised to the power e for e >= 0. State the base case and its value and the recursive case, then trace `pw(3, 4)` showing what is pending in each frame. Show your working.
questions.concept: Writing a recursive power function
Reverse traversal bounds
questions.why:
The legal indices are 0 to 3, but the loop visits i = 4, 3, 2, 1. The first access, a[4], is one past the end: it compiles and runs, and prints whatever junk is stored there. Then a[3], a[2], a[1] print 8 6 4. The loop stops when i reaches 0, so a[0] (the value 2) is never printed. Output: junk 8 6 4. The corrected loop is `for (i = 3; i >= 0; i--) printf("%d ", a[i]);`, which prints 8 6 4 2.

A correct answer says a[4] is out of range and prints an unpredictable value, that a[0] is missed, and starts the loop at 3 and continues while i >= 0. Starting at 3 with i > −1 is also accepted.

questions.concept: Rewriting recursion as a loop
Components of a recursive function
questions.why:
The two components are a base case, which answers the smallest input outright with no recursive call, and a recursive case, which calls the function on a smaller version of the same problem and combines the result. The further condition is progress: every recursive call must move its argument towards the base case. Here the base case (e == 0 returns 1) is present and the recursive case has the right combining work, b × ..., but the call passes e unchanged, so no progress is made. pw(2, 3) calls pw(2, 3) again, forever, each call adding a frame with a multiplication pending, until the stack overflows and the program crashes. The fix is pw(b, e − 1).

A correct answer names base case, recursive case and progress towards the base case, identifies the unchanged e as the failure, and says the result is infinite recursion ending in a stack overflow, not a wrong number.

checks.topic: Popular culture, the four waves of Nigerian music, and the #EndSARS crisis.

questions.q: A Nigerian artist blends reggae and R&B into his sound, is signed by an international label, and is criticised for sounding more American than Nigerian; the labels later leave. Which wave of Nigerian popular music is this?
questions.concept: Identifying a wave of Nigerian popular music
questions.why: The Third Wave (1980-90) is when international labels arrived (Island Records signed Sunny Ade, Virgin signed Ebenezer Obey), artists infused reggae, calypso, rap and R&B, and the music dwindled as the labels left and it sounded more American than Nigerian. The Fourth Wave continued the American-sounding quest but is the rebuilding period with groups like Plantashun Boiz and Psquare; the First Wave was deeply traditional with Ghanaian Highlife and calypso influences; the Second Wave was Highlife's revival, Fela's Afrobeat, Juju and Fuji.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the genres of the Second Wave (1967-80) is correct?
options: Fuji emerged as a fusion of Apala and Ajisari and was mostly for the lower class
Juju, played by Ebenezer Obey and King Sunny Ade, was a song for the lower class
In Ghana, Highlife had been feel-good upper-class music before Nigeria borrowed it
Afrobeat became mainstream through Salawa Abeni
questions.concept: Second Wave genres and their class audiences
questions.why: Fuji emerged as a fusion of Apala and Ajisari, drew major influences from Islam and was mostly for the lower class, with Sikiru Ayinde Barrister and Ayinla Kollington. Juju was a song for the upper class, not the lower. The Highlife point is reversed: in Ghana it addressed social problems, and it was in Nigeria that it became feel-good upper-class music. Afrobeat became mainstream through Fela; Salawa Abeni is the Waka star of the Third Wave.

questions.q: Put these #EndSARS events in the order they happened: (A) the Nigerian Army opens fire on protesters at the Lekki toll gate; (B) #EndSARS begins as a hashtag on Twitter; (C) a video of a police officer shooting an unarmed civilian sparks the crisis; (D) a record 10 million new voters register for the 2023 elections.
questions.concept: Chronology of the #EndSARS crisis
questions.why: The hashtag began on Twitter in 2017 (B); the immediate cause of the October 2020 crisis was the video of a police officer targeting an unarmed civilian (C); the three-week protest ended with the army opening fire at the Lekki toll gate on 20 October 2020 (A); the movement then produced a record 10 million new registered voters for the 2023 elections (D). The first option puts the video before the hashtag, the third puts Lekki before the shooting that triggered the protests, and the fourth puts voter registration before Lekki, when it was the Lekki incident that sent the youth to the polls.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the 2023 elections is correct?
options: Voter turnout was 76%, the highest since independence
Only 40% of registered voters obtained their Permanent Voter Cards
Young people made up 29% of newly registered voters
Voter turnout was 29%, the lowest in Nigeria's six decades of independence
questions.concept: Youth participation and turnout in the 2023 elections
questions.why: Despite huge youth attendance, countrywide turnout was 29%, and no election in Nigeria's six decades of independence has had a lower participation rate. The 76% figure is the share of newly registered voters who were young people, and 40% of those registered as students. Of the 93.4 million registered voters, 87.2 million obtained their Permanent Voter Cards, so the PVC figure is far above 40%.

questions.q: The term popular culture was coined in the mid-19th century. What does it refer to?
options: The official culture of the state and the governing classes
The cultural traditions of the people, in contrast to the official culture of the state or governing classes
Music that requires guided listening by a trained audience
Cultural products created only by the middle class
questions.concept: Definition of popular culture
questions.why: Popular culture refers to the cultural traditions of the people, in contrast to the official culture of the state or governing classes; more broadly it is the traditions and material culture of a society, and in the modern West the music, art, film, television and other products consumed by most of the population. The first option is the opposite of the definition. Popular music is receptive precisely because it does not require guided listening. The middle class created by the Industrial Revolution is where scholars trace the origins of popular culture, but the culture is that of the people at large, not of one class.

checks.topic: Backend work: server-side languages, stacks, choosing a DBMS, and calling REST APIs.

questions.q: A ride-hailing API keeps rides at `/api/rides`. The fare on ride 482 must be corrected. Which request?
questions.concept: Choosing the HTTP method and endpoint for an action
questions.why:
Correcting a field on a ride that already exists is an update, and update is PUT's job. The resource is one specific ride, so the request goes to that ride's own endpoint: PUT /api/rides/482.

POST /api/rides creates a brand-new ride at the collection; GET /api/rides/482 only retrieves it and changes nothing; DELETE removes the ride altogether.

questions.q: An API allows 60 requests per minute per client. A client sends its 61st request within the same minute. Which status code does it receive?
questions.concept: Reading HTTP status codes from an API
questions.why:
Refusing a request because the client has exceeded its quota is rate limiting, and the code for it is 429 (Too Many Requests). The client is identified and the endpoint exists; only the frequency is the problem.

404 means the endpoint or resource was not found; 401 means the client was not authenticated; 503 is a server-side error meaning the service itself is unavailable, not that the client sent too much.

questions.q: A client sends `POST /api/rides` with a valid body and the server creates the new ride. Which status code should the response carry?
questions.concept: Success codes for create versus read
questions.why:
Success codes are in the 2xx range, and 201 (Created) is the one that says a new resource now exists as a result of the request. It is the standard reply to a successful POST that creates data.

200 is the general success code for a satisfied GET; 401 is an authentication failure; 500 is a server error, the opposite of success.

questions.q:
```js
const r = JSON.parse(body);
```
`body` is `{"status": 200, "data": {"id": 482, "driver": {"name": "Ada", "rating": 4.8}}}`. Which expression gives `"Ada"`?
questions.concept: Reading a nested field from a JSON response
questions.why:
JSON.parse turns the text into an object. name sits inside driver, which sits inside data, which sits at the top level, so the path is r.data.driver.name.

r.driver.name skips the data level; r.data.name stops one level short, there is no name directly under data; r.name looks at the top level, which has only status and data. All three give undefined or throw.

options: Line 1: the URL must include the ride id
Line 2: the method should be PUT
Line 3: the header should be text/plain
Line 4: the body must be JSON.stringify({ driver: "Ada" })
questions.concept: Serialising a request body as JSON
questions.why:
A request body travels as text. Passing a plain object makes the browser convert it with toString, which gives "[object Object]". JSON.stringify turns the object into the JSON text {"driver":"Ada"} that the header promises and the server can parse.

The collection URL is right for creating a ride; POST is the create method; the header correctly declares JSON, the problem is that the body does not match it.

questions.q:
Table `customers` holds (id, name, city): (1, Zara, Lagos), (2, Bola, Abuja), (3, Ade, Lagos), (4, Chi, Lagos).
```sql
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lagos' ORDER BY name;
```
What is returned?
questions.concept: Reading a SQL SELECT with WHERE and ORDER BY
questions.why:
